overview: In Amazon Redshift, every table row must live on exactly one node slice. Distribution style (DISTSTYLE) controls how rows are assigned to slices, which determines whether a join can be executed locally on each node or requires an expensive cross-node data shuffle.

Sort keys define the physical order in which rows are stored on disk within each slice. Redshift records the minimum and maximum values stored in each 1 MB block (zone maps), allowing the query engine to skip entire blocks whose range cannot contain qualifying rows.

Choosing the right distribution and sort key combination is the single most impactful physical design decision in Redshift and the primary reason two otherwise identical queries can differ in speed by 10x or more.
learningObjectives: Explain the four distribution styles (KEY, ALL, EVEN, AUTO) and choose the correct one given a table's role in joins.
Describe how COMPOUND and INTERLEAVED sort keys work, including zone maps and block skipping.
Know when to run VACUUM REINDEX and why it is only necessary for INTERLEAVED sort keys.
Diagnose distribution skew and sort order degradation using Redshift system views.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A Redshift distribution style (DISTKEY, DISTSTYLE ALL/EVEN/AUTO) determines which slice stores each row, controlling whether join inputs are colocated; a sort key (COMPOUND or INTERLEAVED SORTKEY) defines the physical ordering of rows on disk per slice and enables zone-map-based block pruning for WHERE clause filters.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine you run a chain of warehouses (node slices) and need to match purchase orders with customer records. If you store both in the same warehouse based on the same customer ID (KEY distribution), the workers in each warehouse can match them locally without any shipping. But if you randomly scatter purchase orders across all warehouses (EVEN), every match requires shipping records between sites — that is redistribution, and it is slow. Sort keys are like organizing shelves alphabetically by date within each warehouse: if you only need orders from June, you can skip all the January-May shelves immediately instead of searching the whole warehouse.
coreConcept.historicalContext: When Redshift launched in 2013, manually choosing distribution and sort keys was the primary performance tuning lever and required expert knowledge of the data model. AWS introduced DISTSTYLE AUTO in 2019 to let Redshift's advisor pick and change distribution styles automatically based on observed query patterns. The same year, AUTO sort keys were introduced. INTERLEAVED sort keys were available from the early days but have fallen out of favor as their VACUUM REINDEX cost became understood; AWS documentation now recommends COMPOUND sort keys for most use cases.

whyItMatters.business: Poorly distributed tables cause queries to take minutes instead of seconds, directly impacting dashboard load times and analyst productivity. The fix — changing a distribution key — requires a table rebuild but is a one-time DBA task that can speed up dozens of downstream queries permanently.
whyItMatters.engineering: Understanding distribution and sort keys is the foundation of Redshift physical data modeling. Engineers who skip this tuning step will consistently produce underperforming schemas, while those who apply it correctly write SQL that the engine executes optimally without query hints.
whyItMatters.scalability: KEY distribution with colocated joins scales with node count: doubling nodes doubles parallelism with no cross-node shuffle. EVEN distribution with non-colocated joins creates an O(n) network shuffle on every join, which becomes a bottleneck at scale.
whyItMatters.cost: Cross-node redistribution wastes compute and network bandwidth. Queries that require redistribution consume 2-3x more cluster resources than colocated joins, meaning you need a larger cluster to sustain the same query throughput. Better distribution keys reduce cluster size requirements.
whyItMatters.reliability: Distribution skew — where one slice receives far more rows than others — causes 'hot slice' problems where one node is a bottleneck while others are idle. This manifests as high variance in query latency and can make SLA guarantees impossible to meet.

coreComponents.name: DISTSTYLE KEY (DISTKEY)
coreComponents.definition: A distribution style that hashes each row's DISTKEY column value and places the row on the slice whose hash bucket matches. Rows with the same DISTKEY value always land on the same slice.
coreComponents.purpose: Colocate rows from two tables that are frequently joined on the same key, so the join executes locally on each slice without redistributing rows over the network.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Assign rows to slices deterministically based on the hash of the DISTKEY column value. Ensure that when two tables share a DISTKEY on the join column, the matching rows from both tables are always on the same slice.
coreComponents.examples: CREATE TABLE fact_orders (order_id BIGINT, customer_id BIGINT DISTKEY, ...) — rows with the same customer_id land on the same slice, so a join to dim_customers with DISTKEY customer_id requires no redistribution.

coreComponents.name: DISTSTYLE ALL
coreComponents.definition: A distribution style that stores a complete copy of the entire table on every node in the cluster.
coreComponents.purpose: Allow small reference/dimension tables to be joined to any table on any node without any redistribution, because a local copy exists on every node.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Maintain full table copies on all nodes. During writes (INSERT/UPDATE), Redshift keeps all node copies synchronized. Accept the trade-off of N times the storage for a table distributed to N nodes.
coreComponents.examples: CREATE TABLE dim_country (country_code CHAR(2), country_name VARCHAR(100), ...) DISTSTYLE ALL — a 200-row country lookup table, copied to all nodes so any join to it is always local.

coreComponents.name: DISTSTYLE EVEN
coreComponents.definition: A distribution style that assigns rows to slices in a round-robin fashion, distributing them as evenly as possible across all slices.
coreComponents.purpose: Provide uniform data distribution when no join colocation is needed, avoiding the risk of distribution skew that can occur with a poorly chosen DISTKEY.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Distribute rows evenly to prevent hot slices and maximize parallel scan throughput. Accept that joins involving an EVEN-distributed table will typically require redistribution.
coreComponents.examples: A staging table used for bulk loads and transformations before data is inserted into a properly distributed production table is a valid EVEN use case.

coreComponents.name: DISTSTYLE AUTO
coreComponents.definition: The default distribution style (since 2019) that lets Redshift automatically pick and change the distribution style based on the table size and observed query access patterns.
coreComponents.purpose: Reduce the operational burden of manual distribution key selection, especially for new tables or tables whose access patterns are not yet well understood.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Initially assigns DISTSTYLE ALL to small tables (< ~1 MB) and DISTSTYLE EVEN to larger tables, then monitors WLM query patterns and may automatically change to KEY distribution if it observes repeated hash joins on the same column.
coreComponents.examples: A new fact table created without explicit DISTKEY or DISTSTYLE gets DISTSTYLE AUTO, and Redshift may transition it to KEY distribution on order_id after observing join patterns.

coreComponents.name: COMPOUND Sort Key
coreComponents.definition: The default sort key type that sorts rows in the order the sort key columns are listed — a strict lexicographic ordering where the first column is the primary sort, the second is a tiebreaker within the first, and so on.
coreComponents.purpose: Enable zone-map-based block skipping for range filters and equality filters on the leading sort key columns, significantly reducing the number of disk blocks read.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Physically order rows on disk by the compound sort key sequence. Maintain zone maps (min/max values per 1 MB block) for efficient block pruning. Become partially unsorted as new rows are appended (requiring VACUUM SORT to restore order).
coreComponents.examples: COMPOUND SORTKEY (order_date, customer_id) — queries filtering on order_date skip blocks whose zone maps show no rows in the date range; a filter on customer_id alone without an order_date filter cannot use the sort key effectively.

coreComponents.name: INTERLEAVED Sort Key
coreComponents.definition: A sort key type that gives equal weight to multiple sort columns using a space-filling curve to interleave the orderings, so filtering on any single column in the sort key can benefit from pruning.
coreComponents.purpose: Support queries that filter on different subsets of the sort key columns with equal frequency, where a COMPOUND sort key would only help queries that filter on the leading column.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Maintain interleaved ordering across all specified columns. Require VACUUM REINDEX (not just VACUUM SORT) to rebuild the interleaved index after data changes, which is significantly more expensive than a standard VACUUM.
coreComponents.examples: INTERLEAVED SORTKEY (customer_id, product_id, region) — a query filtering only on product_id can still prune blocks, whereas a COMPOUND key on (customer_id, product_id, region) would only help filters on customer_id or customer_id + product_id.

internalWorking: When a row is inserted or loaded via COPY, Redshift hashes the DISTKEY column value (for KEY distribution) or applies round-robin (EVEN) or broadcasts (ALL) to determine which slice receives the row. For AUTO, Redshift applies its own policy based on table size.

Within each slice, rows are written in the order they arrive. VACUUM SORT reorganizes them physically on disk into sort key order, and as it does so, it writes or updates the zone map for each 1 MB data block, recording the minimum and maximum sort key values contained in that block.

At query time, when the engine encounters a WHERE clause filter on the leading sort key column, it consults the zone maps. Any block whose [min, max] range does not overlap the filter predicate is skipped entirely — this is block-level pruning and can eliminate 90%+ of I/O for selective range queries on date or ID columns.

For joins, the query planner checks whether the join columns match the DISTKEY columns on both input tables. If they match, the planner uses a colocation join (no data movement). If they do not match, the planner chooses between hash redistribution (sending each row to the correct target slice based on a join-key hash) or broadcast (sending the smaller table to all nodes).

VACUUM REINDEX (for INTERLEAVED sort keys) rebuilds the multi-dimensional interleaved index from scratch using a full table scan, which locks the table and consumes significant cluster resources. VACUUM SORT ONLY (for COMPOUND sort keys) only re-sorts unsorted rows and updates zone maps, which is much cheaper and can be run more frequently.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: INSERT/COPY row -> Hash DISTKEY -> Assign to slice -> Write to unsorted region -> VACUUM SORT -> Sort key order on disk + zone map per block -> Query with WHERE filter -> Zone map check -> Skip non-qualifying blocks -> Scan qualifying blocks only -> Return rows
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A COPY command loads 500 million fact_orders rows. Redshift hashes each row's customer_id (the DISTKEY) and routes it to the slice that owns that hash bucket. After the load, rows are in the unsorted region of each slice.

2. VACUUM SORT runs (or AUTO VACUUM triggers), physically reordering rows within each slice by order_date (the SORTKEY). It writes zone maps for each 1 MB block: block 1 has dates 2020-01-01 to 2020-03-15, block 2 has 2020-03-15 to 2020-06-01, and so on.

3. A dashboard query runs: SELECT SUM(order_value) FROM fact_orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND order_date BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-06-30'. Redshift routes this to the slice owning hash(42). That slice checks zone maps for the order_date range, skipping all blocks outside 2026.

4. A second query joins fact_orders to dim_customers (also DISTKEY customer_id). Since both tables hash customer_id to the same slice, the join executes entirely locally on each slice with no redistribution. The leader node collects the aggregated partial results from each slice.

5. A third query joins fact_orders to fact_inventory (DISTKEY product_id, a different key). The planner detects a key mismatch and chooses to hash-redistribute fact_orders rows by product_id to the correct target slices before joining — visible in EXPLAIN as 'DS_DIST_BOTH' or a Redistribute step.

keyTerminology.meaning: The column designated as the distribution key for a table; Redshift hashes this column's value to determine which slice stores each row.
keyTerminology.importance: The DISTKEY determines whether a join between two tables is colocated (no data movement) or requires redistribution (expensive network shuffle). Choosing the correct DISTKEY is the highest-impact Redshift tuning decision.

keyTerminology.meaning: Metadata stored per 1 MB disk block recording the minimum and maximum values of the sort key column(s) stored in that block.
keyTerminology.importance: Zone maps enable block-level pruning: the engine skips any block whose zone map range does not overlap the query's filter predicate, dramatically reducing I/O for range and equality filters on sorted columns.

keyTerminology.meaning: A query execution step where rows are sent over the internal network to different slices to satisfy a join or aggregation that requires rows with matching keys to be colocated.
keyTerminology.importance: Redistribution is expensive: it consumes CPU, network bandwidth, and memory buffers on every node. A single poorly chosen DISTKEY can cause redistribution on every execution of a high-frequency join, multiplying the cost by the frequency of that query.

keyTerminology.meaning: An imbalance where the DISTKEY column's value distribution causes a disproportionate number of rows to hash to the same slice(s), leaving some slices heavily loaded while others are nearly idle.
keyTerminology.importance: Skewed distribution turns the bottlenecked slice into the performance ceiling for the entire query — parallel processing is only as fast as the slowest slice. High skew can make EVEN distribution faster than a skewed KEY distribution.

keyTerminology.meaning: A Redshift VACUUM variant required for INTERLEAVED sort keys that rebuilds the multi-dimensional sort index from scratch; significantly more expensive than VACUUM SORT ONLY.
keyTerminology.importance: If VACUUM REINDEX is not run regularly on INTERLEAVED sort key tables after data changes, the interleaved index degrades and zone maps lose their pruning effectiveness, eliminating the intended benefit of INTERLEAVED sort keys.

keyTerminology.meaning: A join where the matching rows from both input tables are already on the same slice because both tables have matching DISTKEY columns, allowing the join to execute locally without any cross-node data movement.
keyTerminology.importance: Colocation is the goal of distribution key design. A colocated join scales linearly with node count; a redistributed join adds a fixed per-query network shuffle cost that does not benefit as much from adding nodes.

keyTerminology.meaning: The default sort key type that physically orders rows on disk by multiple columns in the order listed, like a multi-column ORDER BY stored on disk.
keyTerminology.importance: COMPOUND sort keys provide the best pruning for queries that filter on the leading sort key column(s) and are cheaper to maintain (VACUUM SORT) than INTERLEAVED sort keys (VACUUM REINDEX).

keyTerminology.meaning: A sort key type that interleaves the orderings of multiple columns using a space-filling curve so each column has approximately equal pruning power.
keyTerminology.importance: Useful when queries have varied filter patterns across multiple columns with no dominant leading column, but the expensive VACUUM REINDEX requirement makes COMPOUND sort keys preferable in most modern workloads.

importantConcepts.concept: Choosing the Right DISTKEY: Colocation vs Skew Trade-off
importantConcepts.explanation: The ideal DISTKEY colocates frequently joined tables and has high cardinality (many distinct values) to distribute rows evenly across slices. If you choose a low-cardinality column (e.g., region with only 5 values on a 48-slice cluster), most slices get no rows and all data piles onto 5 slices — extreme skew. Check distribution skew by querying SVV_TABLE_INFO or STL_DIST and looking at the skew ratio (max slice row count / average row count). A ratio above 1.5 warrants reconsidering the DISTKEY. When a table joins to multiple tables on different keys, pick the join that runs most frequently or on the largest volume as the colocation target.

importantConcepts.concept: How Zone Maps Enable Block Skipping
importantConcepts.explanation: Redshift stores data in 1 MB blocks on disk. When VACUUM SORT orders the rows by the sort key, rows with similar sort key values end up in the same blocks. Each block's zone map records min(sortkey) and max(sortkey) for that block. When a query has WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-06-30', Redshift reads only the zone maps (a tiny amount of metadata) and skips any block where max(order_date) < '2026-01-01' or min(order_date) > '2026-06-30'. For a table with 5 years of data sorted by order_date, a 6-month filter skips roughly 90% of blocks, turning a 10-minute full table scan into a 1-minute selective scan.

importantConcepts.concept: AUTO Distribution: When to Override It
importantConcepts.explanation: DISTSTYLE AUTO (the modern default) is a good starting point: Redshift picks ALL for small tables and EVEN for large ones, then may upgrade a large table to KEY distribution based on query patterns. The Redshift Advisor (in the console under Recommendations) will suggest an explicit DISTKEY if it observes repeated redistributions on a specific column. You should override AUTO with an explicit DISTKEY when you already know the dominant join pattern (the DISTKEY design is obvious from the schema), for very large fact tables in a star schema, or when the Advisor surfaces a recommendation.

variationsAndTypes: **DISTSTYLE KEY:** Best for large fact tables joined frequently to other tables on the same key. Requires careful cardinality check to avoid skew. Example: fact_orders DISTKEY(customer_id) joined to dim_customers DISTKEY(customer_id).

**DISTSTYLE ALL:** Best for small dimension tables (< ~3 GB) that are joined to many different large tables. Costs N times the storage (one copy per node) but eliminates all redistribution for that table.
**DISTSTYLE EVEN:** Best for staging tables, temporary tables, or tables with no dominant join pattern. Provides perfect load balance but requires redistribution for almost all joins.

**DISTSTYLE AUTO:** The default for new tables. Best for new schemas or teams without deep Redshift expertise; monitor Advisor recommendations and override with explicit KEY once join patterns are established.
**COMPOUND SORTKEY:** Best for range filter queries on a dominant leading column (e.g., order_date, event_timestamp). Cheap to maintain (VACUUM SORT). Default sort key type.

**INTERLEAVED SORTKEY:** Best for ad-hoc queries filtering on multiple different columns with no dominant leading column. Expensive to maintain (VACUUM REINDEX). AWS now recommends exhausting COMPOUND alternatives before using INTERLEAVED.
advantages: **Eliminates redistribution for colocated joins:** When the DISTKEY is correctly chosen, hash joins between large tables execute locally on each slice with zero network overhead, providing linear scale-out as node count increases.

**Zone maps provide free block pruning:** Unlike explicit secondary indexes that must be created and maintained, zone maps are written automatically by VACUUM SORT and reduce I/O dramatically for range filters on sort key columns.

**DISTSTYLE ALL removes redistribution for small dimension tables:** No matter how many large fact tables join to a small dimension table, DISTSTYLE ALL ensures a local copy is always available, eliminating redistribution for those joins.
**AUTO reduces DBA burden:** DISTSTYLE AUTO makes Redshift usable without deep physical design expertise, with Advisor recommendations providing a clear upgrade path when optimizations are needed.
disadvantages: **Wrong DISTKEY causes skew:** A low-cardinality DISTKEY concentrates rows onto few slices, turning a parallel query into a single-slice bottleneck. This is worse than EVEN distribution and harder to diagnose.

**Changing DISTKEY requires rebuilding the table:** To change the distribution style, you must CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) into a new table with the desired DISTKEY. This requires double the storage temporarily and a table rename/swap, causing a maintenance window.

**INTERLEAVED sort keys are expensive to maintain:** VACUUM REINDEX on an INTERLEAVED sort key table performs a full table scan and rebuild, consuming significant cluster resources and taking hours on large tables.

**ALL distribution multiplies storage cost:** A 50 GB dimension table with DISTSTYLE ALL on a 16-node cluster consumes 800 GB of managed storage. As table size or node count grows, the ALL storage multiplier becomes significant.

**Sort key degradation requires VACUUM:** New rows loaded into a sorted table land in an unsorted region. Without VACUUM SORT, zone maps degrade over time and pruning becomes less effective, gradually slowing range queries.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use DISTKEY(join_column) when a table has a dominant high-cardinality join column and its join partner can share the same DISTKEY. Use DISTSTYLE ALL for small stable dimension tables (< ~3 GB) joined to many different fact tables. Use DISTSTYLE EVEN for staging tables or truly scan-heavy workloads with no join partners. Use COMPOUND SORTKEY on the most common range filter column (typically a date or timestamp). Reserve INTERLEAVED SORTKEY for tables with genuinely varied filter patterns across multiple columns where COMPOUND provides no benefit on secondary columns.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid DISTKEY on low-cardinality columns (status, region, boolean flags) — use EVEN instead. Avoid DISTSTYLE ALL on tables larger than ~3-5 GB or tables with frequent heavy writes (every write must update all node copies). Avoid INTERLEAVED SORTKEY unless COMPOUND alternatives have been fully evaluated, because the VACUUM REINDEX maintenance cost is prohibitive on large, frequently-updated tables.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Distribution keys are like partitioning a library's books across multiple branch libraries. If you put books and the index cards for those books in the same branch (KEY distribution, colocation), a researcher can find and read everything in one place. But if you split the books evenly across all branches while putting all index cards in one branch (mismatched distribution), the librarian has to ship books from all branches to the central index every time — that is redistribution. Sort keys are like alphabetically organizing shelves in each branch: if you want books about 2026 events, you can skip the whole 2000-2025 shelf range immediately instead of checking every shelf. DISTSTYLE ALL is like putting a photocopy of a popular reference book (e.g., a dictionary) in every single branch so no one ever has to request it from another location.

commonMisconceptions.myth: DISTKEY should always be the primary key to ensure even distribution.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Primary keys are unique by definition, which does give good distribution but means the join colocation benefit only works for tables with the exact same primary key. The goal is to pick the DISTKEY that collocates the most expensive, most frequent join. In a star schema, the fact table DISTKEY should match the dimension table DISTKEY — not necessarily the primary key of either.

commonMisconceptions.myth: INTERLEAVED sort keys are generally better than COMPOUND because they support more query patterns.
commonMisconceptions.reality: INTERLEAVED sort keys require VACUUM REINDEX — a full table rebuild — to maintain their effectiveness after data changes. On a large, frequently-loaded table, VACUUM REINDEX can take hours and consumes substantial cluster resources. COMPOUND sort keys only require VACUUM SORT, which is incremental and much cheaper. AWS now recommends COMPOUND sort keys as the default and suggests INTERLEAVED only for specific, justified use cases.

commonMisconceptions.myth: DISTSTYLE EVEN is always the safe default because it guarantees uniform data distribution.
commonMisconceptions.reality: EVEN distributes rows uniformly, which is great for scan-only workloads. But for join-heavy workloads, EVEN almost always requires redistribution on every join, consuming significant network and CPU resources. For a large fact table that is frequently joined, a well-chosen DISTKEY with low skew will significantly outperform EVEN distribution despite the distribution study and testing effort.

productionConsiderations.scalability: KEY distribution scales well with node count as long as the DISTKEY cardinality is much higher than the number of slices. Monitor SVV_DISKUSAGE or STL_DIST to detect skew (slice row count standard deviation) and re-evaluate the DISTKEY if the ratio of max-to-average slice rows exceeds 1.5 after an elastic resize changes the slice count.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Distribution skew creates a hot slice that is the query bottleneck; this manifests as high variance in query latency under concurrent load. Catch skew early by querying SVV_TABLE_INFO and checking the skew column before go-live.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: VACUUM operations (both SORT and REINDEX) hold SHARE locks, allowing concurrent reads but blocking writes. Schedule VACUUM during off-peak hours using the Redshift maintenance window or via an AWS EventBridge-triggered Lambda. Enable AUTO VACUUM to handle incremental maintenance continuously.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Key signals: SVV_TABLE_INFO.unsorted (percentage of unsorted rows — should be < 10%), SVV_TABLE_INFO.stats_off (statistics staleness — 0 = current, 100 = very stale), STL_DIST (per-query redistribution step details), SVL_QUERY_REPORT (per-step execution time to identify redistribution as the slowest step). Alert when unsorted > 20% on tables with active range queries.
productionConsiderations.security: Distribution and sort key choices are schema-level metadata decisions with no direct security implications. However, rebuilding tables to change DISTKEYs (via CTAS or ALTER TABLE) must be performed by superusers or table owners; ensure those operations are tracked in the change management log.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Eliminating redistribution via KEY distribution reduces CPU and network consumption, which can defer the need to add cluster nodes. DISTSTYLE ALL adds storage cost per node, so re-evaluate ALL tables after cluster resizes that significantly increase node count. Effective sort keys reduce I/O dramatically for range queries, which translates to lower cluster CPU utilization and enables smaller cluster sizing.

codeExamples.title: Star Schema DDL with DISTKEY, DISTSTYLE ALL, and COMPOUND SORTKEY
codeExamples.overview: Defines a star schema with a fact table using KEY distribution on the join column, dimension tables using ALL distribution for small lookup tables, and COMPOUND sort keys on the most common filter column.
codeExamples.code:
-- Large fact table: DISTKEY on customer_id (primary join column)
-- COMPOUND SORTKEY on order_date (most common range filter)
CREATE TABLE fact_orders (
    order_id        BIGINT        NOT NULL,
    customer_id     BIGINT        NOT NULL DISTKEY,
    product_id      BIGINT        NOT NULL,
    store_id        INT           NOT NULL,
    order_date      DATE          NOT NULL ENCODE az64,
    shipped_date    DATE          ENCODE az64,
    quantity        INT           NOT NULL ENCODE az64,
    unit_price      DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL ENCODE az64,
    order_value     DECIMAL(14,2) NOT NULL ENCODE az64,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id)
)
DISTSTYLE KEY
COMPOUND SORTKEY (order_date, customer_id);

-- Dimension table: ALL distribution (small, stable, joined from many fact tables)
CREATE TABLE dim_customers (
    customer_id     BIGINT        NOT NULL DISTKEY,
    customer_name   VARCHAR(200)  NOT NULL ENCODE lzo,
    email           VARCHAR(254)  ENCODE lzo,
    customer_segment VARCHAR(50)  ENCODE bytedict,
    signup_date     DATE          ENCODE az64,
    country_code    CHAR(2)       ENCODE bytedict,
    PRIMARY KEY (customer_id)
)
DISTSTYLE ALL  -- full copy on every node: join is always local
SORTKEY (customer_id);

-- Small reference table: ALL distribution
CREATE TABLE dim_country (
    country_code    CHAR(2)       NOT NULL,
    country_name    VARCHAR(100)  NOT NULL ENCODE lzo,
    region          VARCHAR(50)   ENCODE bytedict,
    PRIMARY KEY (country_code)
)
DISTSTYLE ALL;

-- Medium dimension table: KEY distribution on product_id
CREATE TABLE dim_products (
    product_id      BIGINT        NOT NULL DISTKEY,
    product_name    VARCHAR(300)  NOT NULL ENCODE lzo,
    category        VARCHAR(100)  ENCODE bytedict,
    brand           VARCHAR(100)  ENCODE lzo,
    unit_cost       DECIMAL(10,2) ENCODE az64,
    PRIMARY KEY (product_id)
)
DISTSTYLE KEY
SORTKEY (product_id);

-- Verify distribution: check slice row counts for skew
SELECT
    t."table"                                 AS table_name,
    t.diststyle,
    t.sortkey1,
    t.skew_rows,   -- max_slice_rows / avg_slice_rows; >1.5 is concerning
    t.unsorted,    -- % of rows in unsorted region; run VACUUM if >10%
    t.stats_off    -- statistics staleness; 0=fresh, 100=stale
FROM SVV_TABLE_INFO t
WHERE t."schema" = 'public'
  AND t."table" IN ('fact_orders', 'dim_customers', 'dim_products')
ORDER BY t.skew_rows DESC;
codeExamples.breakdown: fact_orders uses DISTKEY(customer_id) because the primary join in the star schema is fact_orders JOIN dim_customers ON customer_id. dim_customers uses DISTSTYLE ALL because it is small (< 500 MB) and joined from multiple fact tables — guaranteeing a local copy on every node. The COMPOUND SORTKEY(order_date, customer_id) on fact_orders means queries filtering WHERE order_date BETWEEN ... can prune up to 90% of blocks. The final SVV_TABLE_INFO query surfaces the skew_rows and unsorted metrics to catch distribution problems before they impact production queries.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
table_name     | diststyle | sortkey1   | skew_rows | unsorted | stats_off
---------------+-----------+------------+-----------+----------+----------
fact_orders    | KEY(customer_id) | order_date | 1.02 | 0.00 | 0
dim_customers  | ALL       | customer_id | 1.00 | 0.00 | 0
dim_products   | KEY(product_id)  | product_id | 1.05 | 0.00 | 0
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting that both sides of a join need matching DISTKEYs for colocation — if fact_orders has DISTKEY(customer_id) but dim_customers has DISTSTYLE ALL, the join is still local (because ALL puts a copy on every node). But if both tables have KEY distribution on different columns, a join on the non-DISTKEY column always requires redistribution. Check EXPLAIN output for 'DS_DIST_BOTH' or 'DS_DIST_INNER' labels on join nodes to detect redistribution.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use ENCODE az64 for date, integer, and numeric columns and ENCODE lzo or ENCODE zstd for VARCHAR columns — compression reduces I/O and storage cost. Monitor skew_rows in SVV_TABLE_INFO after initial data loads; if skew_rows > 1.5, consider switching to DISTSTYLE EVEN or choosing a higher-cardinality DISTKEY. Run ANALYZE tablename after the initial bulk load to populate planner statistics.

codeExamples.title: Diagnosing and Fixing Redistribution with EXPLAIN
codeExamples.overview: Shows how to read the EXPLAIN output to identify redistribution steps, compare colocated vs redistributed join plans, and use system views to quantify the cost.
codeExamples.code:
-- Query 1: Colocated join (fact_orders and dim_customers share DISTKEY customer_id)
-- Expected: DS_DIST_ALL or DS_DIST_NONE -- no redistribution
EXPLAIN
SELECT
    c.customer_segment,
    DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) AS order_month,
    SUM(o.order_value) AS total_revenue
FROM fact_orders   AS o
JOIN dim_customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 2, 3 DESC;

/* EXPLAIN output (colocated):
   XN HashAggregate (cost=...)
     -> XN Hash Join DS_DIST_NONE (cost=...)
          Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
          -> XN Seq Scan on fact_orders o (cost=...)
               Filter: (order_date >= '2026-01-01'::date)
          -> XN Hash (cost=...)
               -> XN Seq Scan on dim_customers c (cost=...)
DS_DIST_NONE means no redistribution -- join is colocated! */

-- Query 2: Redistributing join (fact_orders joined on product_id,
-- but fact_orders DISTKEY is customer_id)
EXPLAIN
SELECT
    p.category,
    SUM(o.order_value) AS total_revenue
FROM fact_orders  AS o
JOIN dim_products AS p ON p.product_id = o.product_id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY 1;

/* EXPLAIN output (redistribution required):
   XN HashAggregate
     -> XN Hash Join DS_DIST_BOTH (cost=...)
          Hash Cond: (o.product_id = p.product_id)
          -> XN Seq Scan on fact_orders o   <-- redistributed
          -> XN Hash
               -> XN Seq Scan on dim_products p  <-- redistributed
DS_DIST_BOTH means BOTH sides are redistributed -- expensive! */

-- Check actual redistribution cost for recent queries
SELECT
    q.query,
    q.querytxt,
    r.rows_pre_distrib,   -- rows sent over network
    r.rows_post_distrib,  -- rows received
    r.step,
    r.elapsed_time / 1000000.0 AS elapsed_sec
FROM STL_DIST          AS r
JOIN STL_QUERY         AS q ON q.query = r.query
WHERE q.userid > 1
  AND q.starttime >= DATEADD(hour, -1, GETDATE())
ORDER BY r.rows_pre_distrib DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- Check VACUUM status to know which tables need maintenance
SELECT
    "table",
    unsorted,
    stats_off,
    tbl_rows,
    size AS size_mb
FROM SVV_TABLE_INFO
WHERE "schema" = 'public'
  AND unsorted > 5
ORDER BY unsorted DESC;
codeExamples.breakdown: DS_DIST_NONE in the EXPLAIN output confirms the join is colocated (no redistribution). DS_DIST_BOTH means both join inputs must be redistributed — the most expensive case. DS_DIST_INNER means only the inner (smaller) table is redistributed (broadcast join, acceptable for small tables). DS_DIST_ALL means one input is DISTSTYLE ALL (local copy available, no network shuffle). The STL_DIST query quantifies actual redistribution row counts for recent queries, making the cost concrete. The SVV_TABLE_INFO query identifies tables needing VACUUM (unsorted > 5%).
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
For colocated query: EXPLAIN shows 'DS_DIST_NONE' on the Hash Join node.
For redistributing query: EXPLAIN shows 'DS_DIST_BOTH' on the Hash Join node.
STL_DIST (example):
query | querytxt (truncated)       | rows_pre_distrib | elapsed_sec
------+----------------------------+------------------+------------
12345 | SELECT p.category, SUM...  | 287,432,981      | 42.3
12346 | SELECT c.segment, DATE...  | 0                |  3.1
codeExamples.commonIssues: Teams often see DS_DIST_ALL on the EXPLAIN output and think it means 'full scan' — it actually means the table uses DISTSTYLE ALL and every node has a local copy, so no redistribution is needed. The confusing naming leads engineers to mistakenly 'fix' a fast path. DS_DIST_NONE is the ideal state for colocated joins; DS_DIST_ALL is acceptable and often good for small dimension tables.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: The goal is to eliminate DS_DIST_BOTH for your highest-frequency, highest-volume joins by matching DISTKEYs on both join sides. Use EXPLAIN on all critical production queries during schema design, before data is loaded, to validate the distribution plan. If a join cannot be colocated (e.g., a table joins to two different fact tables on different keys), make the smaller dimension table DISTSTYLE ALL to at least eliminate one side of the redistribution.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: An e-commerce company runs a 500M-row fact_orders table and reports that their daily revenue summary query (joining fact_orders, dim_customers, and dim_products) takes 12 minutes. The team created the tables with default DISTSTYLE EVEN and no explicit SORTKEY. The goal is to reduce the query to under 1 minute.
endToEndExample.inputData: fact_orders: 500M rows, 80 GB, DISTSTYLE EVEN, no SORTKEY. dim_customers: 5M rows, 800 MB, DISTSTYLE EVEN. dim_products: 200K rows, 30 MB, DISTSTYLE EVEN. Dominant query: JOIN fact_orders to dim_customers ON customer_id, filter WHERE order_date BETWEEN (last 90 days).
endToEndExample.architecture: 4-node ra3.4xlarge cluster (48 slices). Redesign involves creating optimized replacement tables, loading data via CTAS, and swapping table names.
processingSteps: 1. Run EXPLAIN on the 12-minute query to confirm it shows DS_DIST_BOTH on both the fact_orders-to-dim_customers and fact_orders-to-dim_products joins.

2. Determine optimal design: fact_orders should be DISTKEY(customer_id) with COMPOUND SORTKEY(order_date) since customer_id is the primary join key and order_date is the primary filter column. dim_customers should be DISTKEY(customer_id) to colocate with fact_orders. dim_products (200K rows, 30 MB) should be DISTSTYLE ALL since it is tiny and joins to multiple tables.

3. Create replacement tables: CREATE TABLE fact_orders_v2 (...) DISTKEY(customer_id) COMPOUND SORTKEY(order_date); then INSERT INTO fact_orders_v2 SELECT * FROM fact_orders ORDER BY order_date (pre-sorting the insert to minimize VACUUM work).
4. Similarly create dim_customers_v2 with DISTKEY(customer_id) and dim_products_v2 with DISTSTYLE ALL.
5. Run ANALYZE on all three new tables to populate statistics.
6. Rename old tables to _backup suffix, rename _v2 tables to production names within a transaction.
7. Re-run EXPLAIN on the revenue query: confirm DS_DIST_NONE for the fact_orders-dim_customers join and DS_DIST_ALL for the dim_products join. Execute and measure.
endToEndExample.output: The revenue query now runs in 58 seconds (down from 12 minutes). The DS_DIST_BOTH redistribution steps are eliminated; the only I/O cost is scanning the filtered 90-day range of fact_orders, which the order_date COMPOUND SORTKEY prunes from a full 80 GB scan to ~20 GB (90 days out of ~3 years).
endToEndExample.monitoring: After go-live, monitor SVV_TABLE_INFO daily for unsorted percentage growth (new orders load into the unsorted region). Set up AUTO VACUUM to handle incremental sorting. Alert if unsorted > 15% (zone map quality degrades). Track query execution time via STL_QUERY for the revenue report and alert if it exceeds 2 minutes.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If the CTAS migration fails mid-way (e.g., disk space exhausted with both old and new tables present), abort the transaction and drop the incomplete _v2 tables. Re-run with a smaller batch or increase cluster storage. If post-migration EXPLAIN still shows DS_DIST_BOTH, verify both tables have the same DISTKEY column name and matching data types (type mismatch disables colocation).
endToEndExample.finalResult: Query time reduced from 12 minutes to 58 seconds (93% reduction). The team documents the DISTKEY and SORTKEY choices in the table DDL comments and adds a weekly VACUUM SORT ONLY job for fact_orders to maintain zone map quality as new orders are loaded daily.

industryUseCases.problem: Large transaction fact tables were joined to merchant and payment method dimension tables on different keys in different analytical queries, causing redistribution on nearly every join and making the data warehouse feel slow for analysts.
industryUseCases.solution: Analyzed the top 20 most expensive queries by CPU time and identified customer_id as the most frequent join key. Rebuilt fact tables with DISTKEY(customer_id). Small dimension tables (payment methods, card networks — <100K rows) switched to DISTSTYLE ALL. Merchant table (2M rows) also switched to DISTKEY(customer_id).
industryUseCases.benefits: Top 10 most expensive queries reduced runtime by 60-80% on average. Cluster CPU utilization dropped from sustained 85% to 45% for the same query workload, allowing the team to avoid a cluster resize.

industryUseCases.problem: A product recommendation model training pipeline queried a 2 billion row user-event fact table filtered by date range, performing full table scans every run because there was no SORTKEY.
industryUseCases.solution: Rebuilt the user-event table with COMPOUND SORTKEY(event_date, user_id). After VACUUM SORT ran, zone maps allowed the pipeline to skip 95% of blocks for any 30-day training window.
industryUseCases.benefits: Pipeline training data query time reduced from 45 minutes to 4 minutes. Reduced S3 RMS data transfer (fewer blocks read from S3 cache miss). Freed significant cluster compute capacity for other analytical workloads.

industryUseCases.problem: As the user base grew, a learner-progress reporting query that joined lesson_completions (5B rows) to user_profiles (20M rows) began taking over 30 minutes due to redistribution and full scans.
industryUseCases.solution: Applied DISTKEY(user_id) to both lesson_completions and user_profiles to colocate the join. Added COMPOUND SORTKEY(completed_at) to lesson_completions for date range filters. user_profiles (3 GB) was borderline for DISTSTYLE ALL but team chose KEY to avoid the ALL storage multiplier across 16 nodes.
industryUseCases.benefits: Query reduced from 30 minutes to 3 minutes. Distribution skew analysis (SVV_TABLE_INFO) confirmed skew_rows of 1.04 — near-perfect distribution — because user_id has 20M distinct values across 192 slices.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Key distribution scales linearly with node count for colocated joins. As you add nodes via elastic resize, the slice count increases, which changes the hash bucket assignments and requires VACUUM to re-sort rows. After elastic resize, run ANALYZE immediately and schedule VACUUM SORT to restore zone map quality. Monitor skew_rows in SVV_TABLE_INFO after each resize to confirm the DISTKEY still distributes evenly at the new node count.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: VACUUM operations (SORT and REINDEX) are interruptible — if a node fails mid-VACUUM, the operation can be restarted. The partially sorted table retains its zone maps for the already-sorted portion. AUTO VACUUM provides continuous incremental maintenance, reducing the need for large manual VACUUM operations that consume cluster resources for hours.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Table rebuilds for DISTKEY changes (CTAS approach) require temporarily double the table storage. Plan rebuilds during low-traffic windows. Use the LOCK TABLE statement to prevent concurrent writes during the rename swap at the end of the CTAS migration, and wrap the rename in a transaction to make it atomic.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: After restoring from a snapshot, VACUUM state is preserved (the restore reconstructs the exact table state including sort order), so zone maps remain valid. However, if the snapshot was taken during a long VACUUM operation, the table may have partially degraded zone maps. After DR restore, run SVV_TABLE_INFO to check unsorted percentages and schedule VACUUM as needed.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: The highest-impact optimization order: (1) eliminate DS_DIST_BOTH redistribution via DISTKEY colocation, (2) enable zone map pruning via COMPOUND SORTKEY on range filter columns, (3) apply column compression encodings (ENCODE az64 for dates/ints, ENCODE lzo/zstd for VARCHAR). These three steps combined can reduce a typical star schema query cost by 90%.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Fewer bytes read per query (via zone map pruning) means fewer CPU cycles, which allows running a smaller cluster. For workloads where most queries filter on a date range, an effective COMPOUND SORTKEY(date_column) can allow downsizing by 1-2 node levels. Monitor S3 RMS reads via CloudWatch PercentageDiskSpaceUsed (DC2) or custom metrics to verify read reduction after SORTKEY implementation.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: DISTKEY and SORTKEY choices are metadata-level decisions with no direct security implications. However, the CTAS migration process (creating new tables, copying data, dropping old tables) requires elevated privileges. Ensure that DDL change scripts are reviewed and logged. Column-level security (GRANT/REVOKE on columns) continues to work correctly after table rebuilds with new distribution styles.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Essential SVV/STL views to monitor: SVV_TABLE_INFO (skew_rows, unsorted, stats_off per table), STL_DIST (redistribution rows and elapsed time per query step), SVL_QUERY_REPORT (per-step breakdown of scan, sort, join, network time), and STL_VACUUM (VACUUM operation history and timing). Build a weekly report from SVV_TABLE_INFO to catch tables whose unsorted percentage is growing and needs attention.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: After a DISTKEY migration (CTAS rebuild), validate row counts: SELECT COUNT(*) must match between old and new table. Validate no data duplication by checking primary key uniqueness. Validate skew_rows < 1.5 in SVV_TABLE_INFO to confirm distribution is working as intended. Run the target queries via EXPLAIN to confirm expected DS_DIST_NONE or DS_DIST_ALL labels before cutting over.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Set CloudWatch alarms on: QueuedQueries sustained > 5 for > 3 minutes (WLM pressure, possibly from expensive redistributing queries). Add a custom CloudWatch metric emitted daily from a Lambda that queries SVV_TABLE_INFO and alerts if any production table has unsorted > 20% or skew_rows > 2.0. Log all DDL changes (CREATE TABLE AS, ALTER TABLE RENAME) to CloudTrail for audit.

recommendedPractices: **Run EXPLAIN on every new query before deploying to production** to verify the join distribution label (DS_DIST_NONE is ideal; DS_DIST_BOTH is a red flag that must be resolved at the schema level).
**Match DISTKEYs on both sides of your most expensive joins.** In a star schema, the fact table and its primary dimension table should share the same DISTKEY column.
**Use DISTSTYLE ALL for dimension tables under ~3 GB.** This is almost always better than EVEN or KEY for small stable lookup tables that are joined from multiple larger tables.

**Use COMPOUND SORTKEY on the most common range filter column** (almost always a date or timestamp). This is the single cheapest optimization to implement and provides dramatic I/O reduction via zone maps.
**Check SVV_TABLE_INFO weekly** for unsorted percentage and skew ratio; both are leading indicators of performance degradation before it manifests as user complaints.
engineeringStandards: Every CREATE TABLE DDL for production Redshift tables must include explicit DISTKEY/DISTSTYLE and SORTKEY annotations, even if the chosen style is EVEN (document it explicitly rather than relying on a default).
DISTKEY and SORTKEY choices must be documented in a comment on the CREATE TABLE statement, including the rationale (e.g., '-- DISTKEY: customer_id — colocates with dim_customers; primary join key').
CTAS migrations for DISTKEY changes must be tested in a non-production clone of the cluster before running on production, with pre/post query benchmarks and row count validation.
designRecommendations: In star schemas, identify the fact table's single most expensive join partner and use their shared foreign key as the DISTKEY for both tables.
For multi-fact-table schemas, pick the DISTKEY that colocates the largest volume joins; accept redistribution on the smaller joins rather than sacrificing the primary join colocation.
When a fact table has no dominant join pattern (many different joins with similar frequency), compare actual query runtimes between KEY and EVEN before committing — EVEN avoids the risk of skew.
Set SORTKEY to the primary range filter column. For multi-predicate queries, use a COMPOUND SORTKEY with the most selective range column first and tiebreaker columns after.
namingConventions: Name the DISTKEY column consistently across joined tables (customer_id in fact and dim, not customer_id in fact and id in dim) to make colocation intent clear and to avoid type-mismatch bugs that break colocation silently.
Add a DDL comment on tables rebuilt via CTAS noting the original table name and the date of the rebuild: '-- Rebuilt 2026-07-01 from fact_orders_v1 to add DISTKEY(customer_id)'.
documentationStandards: Maintain a data model document that lists every production table's DISTSTYLE, DISTKEY column, SORTKEY type, and SORTKEY columns alongside the rationale.
Document which queries benefit from each sort key decision, including the EXPLAIN output showing DS_DIST_NONE before and after the migration.
Record skew_rows values from SVV_TABLE_INFO at table creation and after each major data load to build a historical baseline for anomaly detection.
testingStrategies: Run EXPLAIN on all P0 production queries with the proposed DDL (in a non-production environment loaded with a representative sample) before deploying schema changes.
After any DISTKEY or SORTKEY change, run the top 10 most expensive queries by historical CPU time and compare before/after execution times.
Test VACUUM SORT run time on production-sized data to ensure it completes within the maintenance window. For tables over 500 GB, VACUUM SORT can take 2+ hours.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing a low-cardinality column (e.g., country_code, status, order_type) as the DISTKEY.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: These columns are common join and filter columns, so engineers assume they are good DISTKEY candidates without checking cardinality relative to slice count.
commonMistakes.impact: A DISTKEY on a column with 10 distinct values on a 48-slice cluster puts all rows on 10 slices at most, leaving 38 slices idle. Queries run as slowly as a single-slice table despite being on a multi-node cluster — potentially slower than DISTSTYLE EVEN.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Check cardinality of the candidate DISTKEY column: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT candidate_column) FROM table_name. The cardinality should be >> number of slices (typically 10x or more). For the country_code scenario, use DISTSTYLE EVEN or find a higher-cardinality join key.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing INTERLEAVED SORTKEY for a large, frequently-updated table without planning for VACUUM REINDEX.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The Redshift documentation explains that INTERLEAVED sort keys help queries filtering on multiple columns, which sounds appealing for ad-hoc analytics. Teams implement it and see initial benefits, but do not realize VACUUM REINDEX is required to maintain effectiveness.
commonMistakes.impact: Over weeks, as new rows are loaded, the interleaved index degrades and block pruning becomes ineffective. The table gradually gets slower without any obvious trigger. When the team eventually runs VACUUM REINDEX, it may take hours and monopolize cluster resources, causing a performance impact during business hours.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Default to COMPOUND SORTKEY for the leading filter column. If you observe that queries filtering on a secondary column do not benefit, consider adding it to the compound key in the second position. Use INTERLEAVED only when queries truly distribute equally across multiple filter columns AND you have a maintenance window for regular VACUUM REINDEX.

commonMistakes.mistake: Joining tables with matching DISTKEY column names but different data types, silently breaking colocation.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The DISTKEY column is called customer_id in both tables, but one is BIGINT and the other is INTEGER (or one is VARCHAR and the other is CHAR). Engineers assume matching names means matching types.
commonMistakes.impact: Redshift cannot colocate the join because the hash functions for different types produce different distributions. The join silently falls back to redistribution, and EXPLAIN shows DS_DIST_BOTH despite both tables appearing to have the same DISTKEY column. The query runs 5-10x slower than expected.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Ensure DISTKEY columns on joined tables have identical data types. Use the same type definition in both CREATE TABLE statements. Check with a query against INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS comparing column data_type for the DISTKEY columns on both tables before finalizing the DDL.

commonMistakes.mistake: Never running VACUUM or ANALYZE after daily bulk loads, allowing zone maps and statistics to degrade over weeks.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Teams focus on the ETL pipeline and forget that Redshift requires periodic maintenance (VACUUM for sort order, ANALYZE for statistics) to stay fast. AUTO VACUUM and AUTO ANALYZE exist but may lag on very high-volume tables.
commonMistakes.impact: Unsorted rows accumulate in the unsorted region, zone maps become stale for new rows (new data is effectively unsorted and requires full scan), and planner statistics become stale causing the optimizer to choose suboptimal join orders. A table that was fast at launch progressively slows down over months.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Enable AUTO VACUUM and AUTO ANALYZE (enabled by default for RA3 clusters). Additionally, after large bulk loads (>10% of table rows), explicitly run VACUUM SORT ONLY tablename and ANALYZE tablename to ensure immediate consistency. Monitor SVV_TABLE_INFO.unsorted and stats_off metrics weekly.

comparisonSection.explanation: With matching DISTKEYs on both join tables, rows with the same key are guaranteed to be on the same slice; the join executes locally with zero network overhead (DS_DIST_NONE in EXPLAIN). With EVEN distribution, the planner must redistribute one or both join inputs over the network to colocate matching keys before joining (DS_DIST_BOTH). Redistribution adds 5-50x overhead depending on table size. Use DISTKEY when you have a clear dominant join column with high cardinality.

COMPOUND sort key provides excellent pruning for filters on the leading column (date_col) and moderate pruning for filters on (date_col, secondary_col) together. INTERLEAVED provides approximately equal pruning power for filters on any individual column. However, COMPOUND only requires VACUUM SORT (incremental, fast) while INTERLEAVED requires VACUUM REINDEX (full rebuild, expensive). For most workloads with a dominant date/time filter, COMPOUND is the right choice.

DISTSTYLE ALL puts a full copy of the dimension table on every node, making any join to it local regardless of the fact table's distribution. The cost is N times the storage. DISTKEY matching the fact table colocates the join without storage multiplication but only works for one specific fact table's DISTKEY. For small tables (< ~3 GB) joined from multiple fact tables with different DISTKEYs, ALL is almost always better. For large dimension tables (> 3-5 GB), use DISTKEY matching the primary fact table.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the purpose of a distribution key (DISTKEY) in Redshift?
beginnerQuestions.answer: The DISTKEY determines which slice stores each row by hashing the DISTKEY column value. Its main purpose is to colocate rows from two joined tables on the same slice, so the join can execute locally on each slice without sending rows over the network (redistribution). If both tables in a join have the same DISTKEY column, matching rows will always be on the same slice.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Good answers mention colocation as the goal, hashing as the mechanism, and redistribution as the cost of getting it wrong.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is a zone map and how does it relate to sort keys?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A zone map is metadata stored per 1 MB disk block recording the minimum and maximum values of the sort key column(s) in that block. When a query has a WHERE clause filter on the sort key column, Redshift reads only the zone maps (tiny metadata) and skips any block whose min-max range cannot contain qualifying rows. This block skipping means a query filtering on a date range may read only 5% of a sorted table's blocks instead of scanning all of them.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want to hear: per-block metadata, min/max range, and that block skipping is the benefit. Mention that VACUUM SORT is what writes zone maps by ordering the rows on disk.

intermediateQuestions.question: When would you choose DISTSTYLE ALL over DISTKEY for a dimension table?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Use DISTSTYLE ALL when the table is small (under ~3 GB), stable (infrequent writes), and joined from multiple fact tables that have different DISTKEYs. ALL puts a copy on every node so any join to the table is local regardless of the fact table's distribution. The trade-off is storage multiplication (one copy per node). For a 50 MB country lookup table on a 16-node cluster, ALL costs only 800 MB extra but eliminates redistribution for every join to that table.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Strong answers give the size threshold (~3 GB), the write frequency caveat (ALL updates must sync all node copies), and the 'joined from multiple different fact tables' use case as the clearest signal.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is distribution skew and how would you detect and fix it?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Distribution skew occurs when the DISTKEY column's value distribution concentrates rows on a few slices while others are nearly empty. The bottlenecked slice determines the query runtime, wasting the parallelism of other slices. Detect it via SVV_TABLE_INFO: the skew_rows column shows max_slice_rows / avg_slice_rows; values above 1.5 indicate significant skew. Fix by changing the DISTKEY to a higher-cardinality column or switching to DISTSTYLE EVEN if no good join colocation key exists.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want the mechanism (hot slice bottleneck), the diagnostic tool (SVV_TABLE_INFO skew_rows), and the fix (higher-cardinality DISTKEY or EVEN).

advancedQuestions.question: Your EXPLAIN shows DS_DIST_BOTH on a join between two tables that both appear to have DISTKEY(customer_id). What are the possible causes?
advancedQuestions.answer: Several root causes: (1) The customer_id columns have different data types (e.g., BIGINT in one table, INT in the other) — type mismatches prevent hash colocation. (2) One table's DISTKEY is customer_id but the other's DISTKEY is a different column despite the column name — check actual DISTKEY via SVV_TABLE_INFO. (3) One table is actually DISTSTYLE AUTO and has not yet been promoted to KEY distribution by Redshift. (4) The join predicate casts one side (e.g., CAST(o.customer_id AS VARCHAR) = c.customer_id), which prevents colocation. Check INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS for data types and SVV_TABLE_INFO for actual diststyle.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Advanced answers enumerate multiple root causes including the type mismatch trap. Interviewers look for systematic diagnostic thinking, not just one answer.

advancedQuestions.question: Why is INTERLEAVED SORTKEY now considered risky for large production tables, and when would you still use it?
advancedQuestions.answer: INTERLEAVED sort keys require VACUUM REINDEX — not VACUUM SORT — to maintain their effectiveness after data changes. VACUUM REINDEX performs a full table scan and rebuild, which is O(table size), takes hours on large tables, and consumes significant cluster resources. If VACUUM REINDEX is not run regularly, the interleaved index degrades and block pruning becomes ineffective. I would still use INTERLEAVED in two scenarios: (1) a small-to-medium read-heavy table with genuinely uniform query patterns across multiple filter columns and a predictable maintenance window for REINDEX, or (2) an append-only table that is rebuilt (CREATE TABLE AS SELECT) periodically — the full rebuild is effectively the VACUUM REINDEX step.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Good answers name VACUUM REINDEX specifically (not just 'more maintenance'), explain why it is more expensive, and give justified use cases rather than just saying 'avoid INTERLEAVED always.'

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: You are designing a Redshift schema for a SaaS analytics product. The core tables are events (10B rows, joins to users and organizations), users (50M rows, joins to events and also to a separate subscriptions table), and organizations (5M rows). Most queries filter on event_timestamp and join events to users. How would you distribute these tables?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The primary expensive join is events-to-users. Both tables should share a DISTKEY to colocate that join. user_id is the natural join key. organizations (5M rows, ~800 MB) is borderline for DISTSTYLE ALL — might be acceptable. events should have COMPOUND SORTKEY(event_timestamp) since that is the primary filter column.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: events: DISTKEY(user_id), COMPOUND SORTKEY(event_timestamp, organization_id). users: DISTKEY(user_id), SORTKEY(user_id). subscriptions: DISTKEY(user_id) to colocate with the users join. organizations: DISTSTYLE ALL if under 3 GB (enabling local joins from both events and users without redistribution), otherwise DISTKEY(organization_id) accepting redistribution for the events-to-organizations join. Validate with EXPLAIN that events-to-users shows DS_DIST_NONE.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: You are migrating a 20 TB on-premise Teradata data warehouse to Amazon Redshift RA3. The warehouse has 50 tables, and the team has no prior Redshift experience. Design the distribution and sort key selection process.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Phase 1 — Schema analysis: document all table sizes, primary join relationships (FK-PK pairs), and the top 50 queries by CPU cost from Teradata's query history. Phase 2 — Distribution design: for each table, classify as large fact (> 1 GB), medium dimension (100 MB to 1 GB), or small reference (< 100 MB). Apply DISTKEY(primary_join_column) to large facts, DISTKEY(matching_join_column) to medium dimensions, and DISTSTYLE ALL to small references. Use DISTSTYLE AUTO for tables with unclear join patterns. Phase 3 — Sort key design: for each large fact table, apply COMPOUND SORTKEY(primary_date_column) based on the most common WHERE clause filter in the top 50 queries. Phase 4 — Validate with EXPLAIN on the top 10 queries in a non-production Redshift cluster loaded with a sample dataset.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: AUTO distribution reduces the initial design risk for uncertain tables but may not be optimal from day one — plan to run Redshift Advisor recommendations at 30 and 90 days post-migration. DISTSTYLE ALL for reference tables multiplies storage but eliminates redistribution; acceptable for < 3 GB, re-evaluate at 5 GB. COMPOUND sort keys are cheap to maintain but only accelerate the leading filter column — accept this trade-off over INTERLEAVED due to maintenance complexity.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Start with the minimum node count that handles the current workload. As data grows, RA3 elastic resize adds compute without data movement. Add sort key columns or change distribution styles only when query profiles show specific bottlenecks — avoid premature optimization on tables with low query frequency.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Distribution style controls which slice owns each row (colocation vs shuffle); sort keys control row order on disk within each slice (zone maps enable block skipping).
keyConcepts: DISTKEY(col): hash col value -> assign row to slice; matching DISTKEYs on join tables = colocated join (DS_DIST_NONE).
DISTSTYLE ALL: full copy on every node — small stable dimension tables; zero redistribution for any join.
DISTSTYLE EVEN: round-robin; avoids skew but almost always requires redistribution for joins.
DISTSTYLE AUTO: Redshift picks; starts as EVEN for large tables, may upgrade to KEY based on observed queries.
COMPOUND SORTKEY: physical row order on disk; zone maps per 1 MB block enable block skipping for range filters on leading column.
INTERLEAVED SORTKEY: equal weight to all columns; requires expensive VACUUM REINDEX; use COMPOUND by default.
Zone map: min/max per block; query with WHERE filter skips blocks outside range — dramatic I/O reduction.
VACUUM SORT: re-sort unsorted rows, update zone maps. VACUUM REINDEX: full rebuild for interleaved keys.
formulas: Skew ratio = max_slice_rows / avg_slice_rows; >1.5 is concerning, >2.0 requires action
Block pruning reduction ~ (filter selectivity on sort key) % of blocks skipped
DISTSTYLE ALL storage overhead = table_size_GB * node_count
commands: EXPLAIN SELECT ...; -- look for DS_DIST_NONE (good), DS_DIST_BOTH (fix needed), DS_DIST_ALL (ALL-distributed table, fine)
SELECT "table", diststyle, sortkey1, skew_rows, unsorted, stats_off FROM SVV_TABLE_INFO;
VACUUM SORT ONLY tablename; -- re-sort unsorted rows, update zone maps (compound sort keys)
VACUUM REINDEX tablename; -- full rebuild for interleaved sort keys
ANALYZE tablename; -- refresh planner statistics after bulk loads
SELECT * FROM STL_DIST WHERE query = <query_id>; -- see redistribution rows/time for a specific query
SELECT * FROM SVL_QUERY_REPORT WHERE query = <query_id> ORDER BY elapsed_time DESC; -- per-step timing
interviewPoints: DISTKEY goal = colocation (DS_DIST_NONE in EXPLAIN); wrong DISTKEY = redistribution overhead on every join.
DISTKEY must have high cardinality (>> slice count) to avoid distribution skew.
DISTSTYLE ALL: small tables only (<~3 GB); multiply storage by node count but eliminate redistribution.
Zone maps = min/max per 1 MB block; COMPOUND SORTKEY on date column enables block skipping for range queries.
COMPOUND SORTKEY (cheap to maintain: VACUUM SORT) vs INTERLEAVED (expensive: VACUUM REINDEX); default to COMPOUND.
DISTKEY type mismatch silently breaks colocation — verify column types match on both sides of every join.
quickNotes: DS_DIST_NONE: colocated join (ideal). DS_DIST_BOTH: both sides redistributed (expensive). DS_DIST_INNER: inner table broadcast (acceptable for small tables). DS_DIST_ALL: ALL-distributed table (local copy everywhere).
Changing DISTKEY requires CTAS (CREATE TABLE AS SELECT) + rename swap — plan for a maintenance window and 2x storage temporarily.
skew_rows in SVV_TABLE_INFO = max_slice / avg_slice row count ratio; run this check after every bulk load.
VACUUM SORT is safe to run concurrently with reads (SHARE lock). VACUUM REINDEX is much heavier — schedule during off-peak.
AUTO VACUUM and AUTO ANALYZE are on by default for RA3 clusters but may lag on very large tables — supplement with explicit VACUUM after large bulk loads.

keyTakeaways: Distribution style (DISTKEY/DISTSTYLE) controls whether join rows are colocated on the same slice or require expensive cross-node redistribution — choosing the right DISTKEY for the dominant join is the highest-impact Redshift tuning decision.

DISTSTYLE KEY colocates rows with the same key on the same slice; DISTSTYLE ALL provides a local copy on every node for small dimension tables; DISTSTYLE EVEN distributes rows uniformly but typically requires redistribution for joins.

Sort keys determine the physical row order on disk; Redshift writes zone maps (min/max per 1 MB block) that allow the engine to skip non-qualifying blocks entirely, reducing I/O by 80-95% for selective range queries on the sort key column.

COMPOUND sort keys are the correct default for most workloads — they are maintained by VACUUM SORT (incremental, cheap); INTERLEAVED sort keys require VACUUM REINDEX (full rebuild, expensive) and should only be used in specific, justified scenarios.
Diagnose distribution and sort key problems via EXPLAIN (look for DS_DIST_BOTH labels) and SVV_TABLE_INFO (check skew_rows and unsorted percentages) before and after schema changes.
